_comment: Canonical GitHub repository policy for the repos this account governs. Derived from the two rulesets live on Tamircohen28/tamirs-superpowers (captured 2026-08-19), not from prose — see session-files/ground-truth-rulesets.md. This file is the single source of truth: no SKILL.md, script, or doc may restate a rule, a context list, or a concurrency group found here. Change workflow: edit -> bump `version` -> `bash scripts/check-github-policy.sh` (offline) -> `scripts/github-policy.sh plan` to see live drift.

defaults._comment: Every ruleset targets the default branch through GitHub's ~DEFAULT_BRANCH magic ref. NO LITERAL BRANCH NAME MAY APPEAR ANYWHERE IN THIS FILE. 15 of the 19 governed repos default to one spelling and 4 to the other, so any literal would be wrong on one of those sets, and it would silently stop matching the day a default branch is renamed. scripts/check-github-policy.sh enforces this by scanning every string value in this document.

required_checks._comment: STRICT / 'require branches to be up to date before merging' IS DELIBERATELY OFF. DO NOT TURN IT ON. This is a decision, not an oversight. The development architecture here is objective -> DAG -> parallel workers -> integration -> ONE pull request. With strict_required_status_checks_policy=true, every merge to the default branch invalidates every other open PR's green status and forces a rebuild of all of them: N merges cost O(N^2) CI runs, workers block on each other, and the integration PR can never stay green long enough to land. Correctness is protected instead by required_linear_history (no merge commits sneaking untested combinations in) plus a full CI run on the integration branch before it merges. If you believe this needs to change, change the architecture first.
required_checks.source_note: Required contexts are per-repository and are NEVER global. A context is a CI job name; job names differ per repo, and a name that does not exist in a repo's workflows blocks every PR in that repo forever. The global default is the empty list; each repo opts its own contexts in under `repositories.<owner/repo>.required_checks.contexts`.

overridable_parameters._comment: The closed set of rule parameters a repository may override, and which direction is stricter for each. Keep this NARROW. Opening the whole `parameters` object would make the canonical rulesets a suggestion — any repository could restate any rule and nothing would notice. Add an entry only when a real case appears, and always with its `stricter` direction, because that is what lets a raise be applied cleanly while a lowering has to be acknowledged and is reported on every run.

required_approving_review_count.summary: How many approving reviews a pull request needs before it can merge. The account default is 0 (see the pull_request rule); a repository with outside collaborators may raise it.

rulesets.name: Default Branch - Safety
rulesets._comment: The floor. Nothing here depends on CI existing, so it is safe to apply to a repo on its first day.

rules._comment: The default branch cannot be deleted.
No force pushes. Rewriting published history on the default branch is the one unrecoverable mistake in this workflow.

rulesets.name: Default Branch - PR & CI
rulesets._comment: How change reaches the default branch: through a pull request, with CI green, on a linear history. Apply this only after a CI workflow exists on the default branch — required contexts that no workflow produces would block every PR. KNOWN LIVE DRIFT (2026-08-19): the copy of this ruleset on Tamircohen28/tamirs-superpowers carries a bypass actor — RepositoryRole 5 (repository admin), bypass_mode `always` — which the ground-truth capture did not record. Canonical says `bypass_actors: []`, deliberately: on a single-admin account an always-bypass for admins means every rule below is advisory, and the drift is exactly the kind that a ruleset screenshot hides. The first `github-policy.sh plan` will show removing it; that removal is the user's call to make, not a script's.

rules._comment: Squash or rebase only in effect: the default branch stays a straight line, so `git log` is a readable list of objectives and a revert is a single commit.

`required_status_checks` is EMPTY here on purpose — contexts are resolved per repository from `required_checks` and `repositories.<owner/repo>.required_checks.contexts`, never from this array. check-github-policy.sh fails if this array is ever non-empty.

Zero required approvals AS THE ACCOUNT DEFAULT, because this is a solo-authored account and a self-approval requirement would only be satisfied by --admin bypasses, which would defeat the whole ruleset. The real gate is required_review_thread_resolution: an unresolved review thread — human or bot — blocks the merge. That keeps review meaningful without inventing a second reviewer who does not exist. A repository with outside collaborators raises the count instead of inheriting this: see repositories.<owner/repo>.required_approving_review_count below, where tamirs-superpowers sets 1 so the requirement binds COLLABORATORS while the owner keeps merging through the repository-admin bypass. The two are one policy, not a contradiction — read them together before changing either. require_extra_approval_for_unattributed_changes is recorded as true because GitHub supplies it on every ruleset and defaults it to true: the parameter did not exist when this file's ground truth was captured on 2026-08-19, so omitting it made the repository report NON-COMPLIANT forever on a field no write can change — GitHub re-supplies the default, and true is the stricter value in any case. Measured 2026-09-01 across 12 repositories on this account, including ones this policy had never been applied to: all true.

repositories._comment: Per-repository overrides, keyed by owner/repo. An absent repo inherits the defaults above with an empty required-context list — protected, but not gated on checks it does not have.

Tamircohen28/tamirs-superpowers._comment: 9 of this repo's CI jobs are required. Adding a CI job does NOT make it blocking; its `name:` must be added to this list and applied.

pull_request._comment: 1, not the account default of 0, and this is deliberate — do NOT 'fix' it back to match the default. This ruleset carries a repository-admin bypass actor, so the requirement binds COLLABORATORS while the owner still merges through the bypass. Read together, the two say: anyone else's change needs a review; the owner keeps an escape hatch on their own repository. Setting it to 0 here would not simplify anything, it would remove the only review requirement that applies to anyone but the owner. This is a raise above canonical, so it applies cleanly and needs no weakening acknowledgement.

actions._comment: GitHub Actions concurrency standard. Cancelling a superseded run is free money on a test workflow and data loss on a deployment, so the classification below is data a script can act on, not advice.

concurrency._comment: The canonical block for a cancellable workflow. Keyed on the PR number when the event is a pull_request, and on the ref otherwise, so pushes to the default branch serialize per-ref instead of colliding with PR runs.

serialize_concurrency._comment: For a never-cancel workflow that still must not run twice at once (a deploy, a release). Same group, cancellation OFF: the second run queues behind the first instead of killing it.

workflow_classification._comment: Classify a workflow by matching its name/filename against `name_patterns` and its file content against `content_signals`. Matching is case-insensitive: lowercase the subject before testing, patterns are stored lowercase. Patterns are POSIX/oniguruma regexes compatible with jq `test()`.
workflow_classification.precedence_note: If a workflow matches signals in both classes, it is never_cancel. A test job wrongly serialized costs minutes; a deploy wrongly cancelled costs a half-written external state.
workflow_classification.unclassified_note: A workflow matching neither class is reported for a human decision and left untouched. Guessing on an unknown workflow is exactly how a migration gets cancelled mid-run.

cancellable.summary: Pure, repeatable verification. Killing a run mid-flight leaves nothing behind but a cancelled check, and the newer commit's run supersedes it anyway.

content_signals.description: runs on pull_request — the event whose runs are superseded by a newer push

never_cancel.summary: Anything that mutates state outside the repo. A cancelled run leaves that external state half-written — a half-published package version, a tag with no release, a migration applied to some tables, an environment pointing at an artifact that was never uploaded. There is no 'just re-run it' for these.
never_cancel.concurrency_note: Never set cancel-in-progress: true on these. If two runs must not overlap, use `serialize_concurrency` so the second queues.

content_signals.description: triggered by a GitHub release event
triggered by tag pushes — a release path
declares a deployment environment, so a run has an external target
requests an OIDC token — it is about to authenticate to a cloud provider

content_signals.pattern: (npm publish|yarn publish|pnpm publish|cargo publish|twine upload|gem push)
content_signals.description: publishes a package to a registry

content_signals.pattern: (aws (s3 sync|cloudformation deploy|ecs update-service)|gcloud (run deploy|app deploy)|az webapp)
(alembic upgrade|prisma migrate deploy|flyway migrate|rails db:migrate|supabase db push)
